title: POC Weekly: VPC egress routing, quantization tuning, and kernel rollback plan
summary: Weekly POC sync covering recent egress routing failures, quantization experiments (4-bit/8-bit), a proposed kernel rollback window for the upgraded runtime, and next steps for logs and benchmark artifacts. Agreed to run a targeted 8k-token perf run, share egress ACL traces, and schedule a short maintenance window to test kernel rollback on staging.
next_steps: Diego to run 8k token quantization perf test and upload logs to shared folder by 2025-08-15.
Marcus to provide traceroute, iptables and egress ACL logs for 2025-08-09 incident by 2025-08-12.
Maya to send pilot pricing snapshot and dedicated capacity options by 2025-08-14.
Schedule 2-hour maintenance window for kernel rollback on staging next Tuesday (2025-08-19) - tentative.
action_items: Diego Ramirez (Redwood) - Run focused 8k-token QAT/4-bit and 8-bit runs and deliver logs + perf csv - due 2025-08-15
Marcus Lee (OrionMed) - Export egress ACLs, traceroutes, and pod logs for the 08-09 failure and share to S3 link - due 2025-08-12
Maya Patel (Redwood) - Share updated pilot pricing and dedicated capacity options and the recommended config for prefix caching - due 2025-08-14
Ellen Zhao (OrionMed) - Confirm internal approval for short staging window for kernel rollback - due 2025-08-13
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-11 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Aria (CSM) — Ellen, Priya, Marcus, Tom (Orionmed)

Summary (auto): Quick sync on egress routing flakes seen last week, review of quantization perf numbers, and plan for a controlled kernel rollback to isolate regression introduced in runtime v1.12.

00:00:05 Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for squeezing this in, I know it's a busy week. Quick roll call?
00:00:12 Ellen Zhao: Ellen here.
00:00:14 Priya Shah: Priya.
00:00:16 Marcus Lee: Marcus.
00:00:18 Tom Rivera: Tom.
00:00:20 Maya Patel: Great. From Redwood we have Diego and Aria on the line as well. Diego do you want to kick off with the egress recap?
00:00:28 Diego Ramirez: Yeah, sure. So, quick context — last Friday around 03:40 UTC you saw ~20% of requests to the private pool fail with egress timeouts when hitting our model shard. The trace we have shows a connection reset between the customer VPC egress NAT and the dedicated node, possibly transient BGP or firewall rate limiting. I ran a few synthetic flows from our side and also from the staging pe, um, staging agent, and didn't fully reproduce the exact socket reset pattern.
00:01:05 Priya Shah: Just to add, our side saw a flurry of rejected SYNs on the NAT gateway and then a spike of retransmits. We also had a few pods that flapped; kube- — cube Nates showed restarts but not backing this out to the NIC.
00:01:20 Diego Ramirez: Right, cube-Nates logs looked like they were, uh, unhappy but primarily on the egress path. Marcus, were you able to pull the iptables dump from the jump host?
00:01:29 Marcus Lee: Yes, I did. I put a copy in the S3 bucket — the file is trace-egress-20250809.tar.gz. I also included the collector trace and the NAT gateway metrics. There's a few ACL rules that coincide with a spike of flows, looks like we have TTL-based cleanup on the firewall that might be happening.
00:01:45 Tom Rivera: We didn't change anything but there was an automatic security policy update pushed last Thursday morning. I flagged it but didn't think it would affect established flows.
00:01:54 Diego Ramirez: That could be the vector. Firewall policy updates + high connection churn sometimes cause transient drops; our runtime will retry once but if the retry window hits the higher-level client deadline you'll see the failure.
00:02:10 Maya Patel: Important for us is whether this is a config/routing issue on OrionMed side or something the runtime changes in 1.12 exposed. On that note — Diego, you ran quantization perf tests last night, right? What did you see?
00:02:21 Diego Ramirez: Yep. I ran baseline 16-bit FP then 8-bit and 4-bit QAT experiments with the same workload. With 8k tokens the 4-bit configs show roughly 1.6x token throughput improvement in ideal local runs, but in the presence of high connection churn we saw KV cache miss amplification — because the quantized kernel's cache alignment is a bit different and we saw slightly higher SKIP rates for prefetched KV chunks. That means more network calls for KV refill in some sequences. It's subtle, but with frequent short-lived connections it could exacerbate egress pressure.
00:03:00 Ellen Zhao: So are you saying quantization could make egress worse? That's not what we expected. Our aim was to reduce cost and keep latency stable.
00:03:10 Diego Ramirez: It's workload dependent. In steady state you get clear wins; in high turn-over connection patterns the prefet- prefetch heuristics may cause more small-range KV fetches. We're looking at tuning the prefetch window and also a hybrid quant profile that keeps hot KV in higher-precision to avoid refetch churn.
00:03:30 Priya Shah: Interesting. Would that be a config we can change on the fly without redeploying kernels?
00:03:35 Diego Ramirez: Most of it is runtime config — you can adjust prefetch_window and cache_ttl live for the serving nodes. The kernel binary change is separate only if we change quantization blocks.
00:03:45 Marcus Lee: If we can avoid rolling the kernel that would be preferable. Last upgrade to 1.12 coincided with the incident so we'd like to be conservative.
00:03:54 Maya Patel: Right, that was our thought — propose two parallel tracks: (1) collect customer logs and egress traces to rule out network config; (2) run targeted perf tests with quantization knobs changed to see if we can reproduce the egress amplification. If both point at kernel/regression then plan a rollback window.
00:04:10 Ellen Zhao: Sounds reasonable. On the rollback — what exactly are we proposing? Full rollback of runtime to 1.11 or a narrow kernel swap?
00:04:18 Diego Ramirez: We can do a narrow kernel swap in staging first — it's basically replacing the GPU kernel binary that v1.12 shipped with the v1.11 artifact and running the same canary. That avoids touching orchestration. If staging is good we can plan a controlled rollback in production in a short maintenance window and route a small percentage of traffic to fallback nodes.
00:04:36 Tom Rivera: Security ask — we need the rollback plan documented with timeline and a blameless postmortem template. Also need to ensure all audit logs remain intact when switching kernels.
00:04:47 Aria Novak: We'll add the rollback steps and timeline to the pilot playbook and ensure audit logging is preserved; our private control plane writes audit to your S3 and to our KMS-backed archive.
00:04:58 Priya Shah: Diego, can you clarify the KV cache behavior? Is this only for certain model families or across the board?
00:05:04 Diego Ramirez: Mostly transformer-backbone models with large per-token KV state — think long-context summarization and multi-turn chat where prefix reuse is nontrivial. Short queries, not so much. The effect shows up with 4k+ context and a lot of warmed/unwarmed connections.
00:05:20 Ellen Zhao: For our use case we have variable context lengths — but many of our long-read threads are 6k to 8k tokens.
00:05:26 Diego Ramirez: Then the 8k targeted test is the right stress case.
00:05:31 Maya Patel: Marcus, you said you uploaded the traces — do you see correlation between the NAT policy rollout and the spike times?
00:05:38 Marcus Lee: Yes. The timestamps align within the TTL modification window — the firewall vendor's policy change ran at 03:30 and we saw the first client-side retransmit spike at 03:38.
00:05:47 Tom Rivera: That aligns with our change. We can revert the policy, but it's managed centrally and needs approval.
00:05:52 Ellen Zhao: If reverting is an option, do we want to try that before scheduling a runtime rollback?
00:05:57 Diego Ramirez: We recommend capturing the artifacts and running the quant tests first. If reverting the firewall is low-friction and quick, it could help, but we also want to know whether the kernel change meaningfully amplified the problem because even with firewall fixes the next similar change could re-expose it.
00:06:15 Priya Shah: Makes sense. Can Redwood produce a short runbook for the prefetch_window and cache_ttl settings you mentioned?
00:06:20 Diego Ramirez: Absolutely — I'll include a config snippet and suggested safe ranges. Example: prefetch_window: 4-8 (default 6), cache_ttl: 30s-120s depending on request churn. We'll put recommended values in the doc.
00:06:33 Maya Patel: For next steps can we align on deadlines? Marcus — get us the full S3 link and traceroute by Tuesday EOD?
00:06:42 Marcus Lee: Yep, Tuesday EOD is fine.
00:06:45 Maya Patel: Diego, 8k runs and logs by Friday?
00:06:49 Diego Ramirez: I'll aim for Friday 08-15 and will push CSVs and perf traces to the shared folder.
00:06:54 Maya Patel: I'll send the pilot pricing snapshot and the dedicated capacity options by Thursday. Also scheduling: we propose a 2-hour staging window 2025-08-19 for kernel swap and a short production window on 08-21 pending staging results. Ellen, can you confirm internal ok for the windows?
00:07:08 Ellen Zhao: I'll check and get back by Wednesday.
00:07:11 Tom Rivera: Quick question on canary routing — would Redwood be able to route 10% of traffic to the fallback nodes while leaving 90% on the upgraded runtime?
00:07:18 Diego Ramirez: Yes, our smart routing layer supports percentage-based traffic splits and automatic fallback based on error budgets. We'll instrument per-route latency and error counts to ensure the canary doesn't exceed thresholds.
00:07:30 Priya Shah: Any implications for tokens billing or cost while we run these extra canaries?
00:07:35 Maya Patel: We'll include a cost delta estimate in the pricing snapshot; canaries at 10% for a short window are usually minor but we'll put numbers against it.
00:07:44 Marcus Lee: Also, can you confirm that audit logs during the rollback will not contain PII in the logs we receive? Security raised that concern.
00:07:52 Aria Novak: Our default audit entries are request IDs, route IDs, timestamps and perf metrics. We do scrub full request payloads from the control plane logs; we can supply a redact policy and sample audit entry.
00:08:05 Tom Rivera: Good.
00:08:07 Diego Ramirez: One other note — in the perf runs I'm going to include a disabled prefetch baseline and a hybrid profile where top-10 hottest KV keys are kept at higher precision. That will let us see if targeted hot-key protection reduces network refetches.
00:08:21 Priya Shah: Fantastic. Will that require model changes?
00:08:24 Diego Ramirez: No, purely serving-side config.
00:08:26 Maya Patel: Alright, let's do quick risk recap and close. Risks: 1) firewall policy revert might be blocked by security process; 2) kernel rollback, even narrow, could impact throughput briefly if misapplied; 3) cost impact of extra canary traffic. Mitigations: collect artifacts, run perf tests, staging swap, documented rollback steps, and short canary windows.
00:08:50 Ellen Zhao: Agree.
00:08:53 Maya Patel: Anything else before we wrap?
00:08:55 Tom Rivera: Just please call out the exact S3 paths once available.
00:08:59 Maya Patel: Will do. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in writing with the artifacts and schedule.
00:09:05 END OF CALL

References and artifacts: Deck (shared): https://redwood.link/pilot-orionmed-deck | Traces bucket: s3://orionmed-pilot/traces/trace-egress-20250809.tar.gz | Config snippet (example): https://redwood.link/configs/prefetch-snippet.md

Note: transcription contains occasional misheard items ("cube-Nates" for Kubernetes), and speaker overlaps were collapsed.
